moments.title: Bi Sheng's clay movable type
moments.body:
Bi Sheng's clay type allows reusable printing characters, centuries before Gutenberg.

Korean metal type follows in the 13th century.
moments.takeaway: The history of printing is not linear from Europe outward.

moments.title: Gutenberg Bible
moments.body: Gutenberg integrates metal-alloy movable type, oil-based ink and an adapted press into a commercially viable system.
moments.takeaway: An integrated workflow, not a single invention, drove the European print revolution.

moments.title: Roughly 8-10 million books printed in Europe
moments.body:
By 1500, presses across Europe have produced approximately 8 to 10 million books (Febvre and Martin, 1958).

The rise of vernacular publishing follows.
moments.takeaway: The volume of printed material exploded within fifty years of Gutenberg.

now.title: Print and after
now.body: Print persists alongside digital media. Newspaper economics are challenged; book publishing remains substantial. Misinformation studies often draw on print-era precedents.
now.open_questions: How should public access to printed and digital archives be preserved over centuries?

items.reflection: Eisenstein and others have argued the print revolution restructured scientific, religious and political life. Comparable claims about the internet are still being tested.

moments.title: First scheduled commercial broadcast
moments.body: KDKA broadcasts US presidential election returns on 2 November 1920, often cited as the start of regular broadcast radio.
moments.takeaway: Broadcasting began at the intersection of news and election politics.

moments.title: British Broadcasting Company formed
moments.body: John Reith leads the BBC, initially a private company, then a public corporation from 1927. The licence fee model is introduced.
moments.takeaway: Public-service broadcasting was a deliberate institutional choice, not an inevitable default.

moments.title: War of the Worlds broadcast
moments.body: Welles's adaptation of H.G. Wells's novel is later wrongly remembered as causing widespread panic. Audience was smaller and reaction more measured than the legend.
moments.takeaway: Media history is itself shaped by competing media industries.

now.title: Broadcasting today
now.body: Linear broadcast competes with streaming and podcasts. Public-service models face political and economic pressure across democracies.
now.open_questions: How can public-service media missions be sustained in a fragmented audience environment?

items.reflection: Decisions made in 1920s broadcasting still constrain how media markets are structured a century later.

moments.title: BBC television service begins
moments.body: The BBC launches the world's first regular high-definition television service. Broadcast resumes after World War II in 1946.
moments.takeaway: Television was a technology of the late 1930s, paused by war and resumed in the 1940s.

moments.title: Cultivation theory
moments.body: Gerbner and Gross argue heavy television viewing cultivates a 'mean world' perception of risk.
moments.takeaway: Long-term media exposure can shape beliefs about social reality.

moments.title: Netflix streaming launches
moments.body: Streaming begins as a bundled feature of the DVD service. The shift towards on-demand viewing accelerates.
moments.takeaway: Companies can pivot business models while running both in parallel for years.

now.title: Audiovisual media today
now.body: Streaming, social video and AI-generated content compete for attention. Measurement and audience research have to reorganise around individual rather than household consumption.
now.open_questions: How will the line between professional and user-generated audiovisual content evolve?

items.reflection: Watching together used to be the default mode of television. The individual screen has become the default unit of audience.

moments.title: World Wide Web public
moments.body: The first website goes online in August 1991. CERN releases the underlying code into the public domain in 1993.
moments.takeaway: Releasing the web protocol openly shaped what followed.

moments.title: Facebook launched
moments.body:
Facebook launches as a Harvard student directory in February 2004.

YouTube follows in 2005, Twitter in 2006.
moments.takeaway: Mass social platforms originated as small student projects within months of each other.

moments.title: Cambridge Analytica revelations
moments.who: Journalists at The Observer, New York Times
moments.body: Reporting reveals harvesting of Facebook profile data for political profiling, leading to public hearings and fines.
moments.takeaway: Platform-level data flows became a subject of mainstream political concern.

now.title: Platforms today
now.body: Generative AI, content moderation and platform regulation (EU Digital Services Act 2022) shape the current landscape. Questions of algorithmic accountability are unresolved.
now.open_questions: How should platform governance be balanced between national jurisdictions and global user bases?

items.reflection: Social media's history is short by media-history standards, but the institutions built around it are now planetary in scale.

moments.title: London Gazette
moments.body: The Oxford Gazette (later London Gazette) becomes the first official English newspaper, still published today.
moments.takeaway: State news organs are among the oldest media institutions.

moments.title: The Times founded
moments.body: The Daily Universal Register becomes The Times in 1788, eventually defining UK newspaper of record.
moments.takeaway: Brand authority builds over centuries.

moments.title: Daily Mail launched
moments.body: The Mail at a halfpenny pioneers mass-market journalism with shorter stories and sensational headlines.
moments.takeaway: Tabloid journalism was an industrial innovation.

now.title: Press today
now.body: Print circulation has collapsed; digital subscriptions and philanthropy partially substitute. Local news 'deserts' raise democratic concerns.
now.open_questions: What replaces local newspapers as civic infrastructure?

items.reflection: Mass-market press shaped public opinion long before social media did.

moments.title: Daguerreotype announced
moments.body: France purchases Daguerre's process and gives it to the world.
moments.takeaway: Photography arrived as a state-sponsored gift.

moments.title: Brady's Civil War photographs
moments.body: Brady exhibits photographs of Civil War dead in New York. 'Mr. Brady has done something to bring home to us the terrible reality and earnestness of war'.
moments.takeaway: Photography reshaped war reportage.

moments.title: Migrant Mother
moments.body: Lange's FSA photograph becomes the defining image of the Great Depression.
moments.takeaway: State-sponsored documentary photography shaped national memory.

now.title: Documentary today
now.body: Photojournalism continues despite industry contraction. AI-generated images challenge photographic truth claims.
now.open_questions: Will photographs retain evidential value when synthesis is trivial?

items.reflection: Pictures have carried evidence for nearly two centuries; we are renegotiating that compact.

moments.title: Lumiere brothers' first public screening
moments.body: Ten short films are shown to a paying audience at the Salon Indien du Grand Cafe on 28 December 1895.
moments.takeaway: Cinema began as a paid public spectacle.

moments.title: A Trip to the Moon
moments.body: Melies's 14-minute film uses elaborate special effects to depict a journey to the moon.
moments.takeaway: Cinema was inventing narrative and special effects in parallel.

moments.title: The Birth of a Nation
moments.body: Griffith's epic introduces cinematic techniques and celebrates the Ku Klux Klan, prompting protests led by the NAACP.
moments.takeaway: Cinema's technical innovations and political content travel together.

now.title: Early cinema today
now.body: Restored prints circulate via Cinematheque Francaise and BFI. Silent film festivals revive period scoring.
now.open_questions: How should we contextualise canonical but harmful films?

items.reflection: Cinema was born as both art and propaganda.

moments.title: The Jazz Singer
moments.body: The first feature-length talking picture transforms the industry within two years.
moments.takeaway: Technology transitions can move at industrial speed.

moments.title: Hays Code enforced
moments.who: Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America
moments.body: The Production Code constrains Hollywood content for three decades.
moments.takeaway: Self-regulation shaped what audiences could see.

moments.title: Paramount Decree
moments.body: The studios are forced to divest their theatre chains, ending the classical studio system.
moments.takeaway: Antitrust law reshaped Hollywood's structure.

now.title: Studio system today
now.body: Streamers like Netflix and Amazon recreate vertically integrated content businesses.
now.open_questions: Are we re-entering a new studio era under streaming?

items.reflection: The 1948 decree was reversed in 2020; vertical integration is back.

moments.title: Bonnie and Clyde
moments.body: The film's stylised violence and moral ambiguity mark New Hollywood's arrival.
moments.takeaway: Hollywood reinvented itself under new directors in the late 1960s.

moments.title: The Godfather
moments.body: Coppola's epic redefines what mainstream Hollywood film can achieve.
moments.takeaway: Director-driven blockbusters built a generation of auteurs.

moments.title: Star Wars
moments.body: Lucas's film returns Hollywood to the blockbuster era, with merchandise revenue exceeding box office.
moments.takeaway: Movies became merchandising platforms.

now.title: Film industry today
now.body: Box office is dominated by franchises and remakes. Independent film faces distribution challenges.
now.open_questions: Is theatrical cinema sustainable when most viewing is at home?

items.reflection: Each generation of Hollywood believes itself the end of the studio era.

moments.title: FDR's first fireside chat
moments.body: FDR's banking address on 12 March 1933 establishes the intimate radio presidential style.
moments.takeaway: Radio rewrote political speech.

moments.title: Murrow at Buchenwald
moments.body: Murrow's broadcast from the liberated camp ends 'I pray you to believe what I have said about Buchenwald.'
moments.takeaway: Radio reporting brought atrocity into living rooms.

moments.title: Murrow on McCarthy
moments.who: Edward R. Murrow, See It Now
moments.body: Murrow's televised critique of Senator McCarthy contributes to the senator's political fall.
moments.takeaway: Television journalism could face down national hysteria.

now.title: Broadcast journalism today
now.body: Cable news, podcasts and streaming reshape the news landscape. Trust in journalism has fallen across democracies.
now.open_questions: Where does authoritative journalism live now?

items.reflection: Radio gave 20th-century leaders a voice in your kitchen.

moments.title: ITV launches
moments.body: Commercial television begins in the UK, with regional franchises and a public-service remit.
moments.takeaway: Commercial and public service coexisted from the start of UK ITV.

moments.title: Colour TV in UK
moments.body: BBC2 begins colour broadcasting; BBC1 and ITV follow in 1969.
moments.takeaway: Colour shifted both production and audience expectations.

moments.title: Channel 4 launched
moments.body: Channel 4 commissions programmes from independents and serves a remit for innovation and diverse audiences.
moments.takeaway: Public-service TV expanded by adding new structures, not replacing old.

now.title: UK television today
now.body: Channel 4 privatisation was reversed in 2022. BBC licence fee debates continue.
now.open_questions: What is the next UK public-service television settlement?

items.reflection: Public-service TV is a political settlement, renegotiated every generation.

moments.title: Tet Offensive coverage
moments.body: Cronkite's reporting from Vietnam shifts US public opinion. LBJ reportedly says 'if I've lost Cronkite, I've lost middle America'.
moments.takeaway: Television journalism shifted national consensus.

moments.title: CNN launches
moments.body: Cable News Network begins 24-hour news, transformed by the 1991 Gulf War broadcast.
moments.takeaway: Continuous news reshaped political tempo.

moments.title: Al Jazeera launches
moments.body: An Arabic 24-hour channel offers regional perspectives that disrupt Western news monopoly.
moments.takeaway: Non-Western news organisations reshape global media flows.

now.title: News today
now.body: Streaming and social platforms compete with traditional channels. News deserts grow in local markets.
now.open_questions: Who funds investigative journalism in the platform era?

items.reflection: 24-hour news made every hour deadline-time.

moments.title: Understanding Media
moments.body: McLuhan's book popularises 'the medium is the message' and 'global village'.
moments.takeaway: Media theory entered popular vocabulary.

moments.title: Encoding/Decoding model
moments.body: Hall theorises three audience positions: dominant, negotiated and oppositional readings.
moments.takeaway: Cultural studies moved audience theory beyond passivity.

moments.title: Uses and Gratifications
moments.who: Jay G. Blumler and Elihu Katz
moments.body: The theory reframes audiences as active seekers of needs, not passive recipients.
moments.takeaway: Audience theory keeps redefining who is in charge.

now.title: Media theory today
now.body: Network theory, platform studies and political economy approaches dominate academic debate.
now.open_questions: Which 20th-century theories still apply to platforms?

items.reflection: How we think about media is itself shaped by the media of our era.

moments.title: Sony Walkman
moments.body: The portable cassette player makes private music listening in public spaces routine.
moments.takeaway: Personal devices reshape public soundscapes.

moments.title: MTV launches
moments.body: MTV begins with 'Video Killed the Radio Star'. Music videos become a mass form.
moments.takeaway: Music marketing reshaped around the visual.

moments.title: Napster
moments.body: Napster's peer-to-peer music sharing collapses CD sales and prompts the iTunes Store (2003).
moments.takeaway: Music industries can change in months under technological shocks.

now.title: Music industry today
now.body: Streaming dominates revenue. Spotify and Apple Music shape what gets heard.
now.open_questions: How do artists earn a living when streams pay fractions of a cent?

items.reflection: Music distribution has changed more in 25 years than in the previous 100.

moments.title: Pong released
moments.body: Pong's commercial success launches the arcade and home console era.
moments.takeaway: Video games became commercial media within months of laboratory existence.

moments.title: Super Mario Bros
moments.body: The NES launch title sells 40 million copies and rebuilds the US video game market after the 1983 crash.
moments.takeaway: Single titles can resurrect industries.

moments.title: PlayStation launches
moments.body: Sony's CD-ROM console targets older players and overtakes Nintendo by the late 1990s.
moments.takeaway: Console wars reflect broader media-industry power.

now.title: Games today
now.body: Games revenue exceeds film and music combined. Live-service games and esports reshape the industry.
now.open_questions: Are games the dominant 21st-century medium?

items.reflection: What started as a bouncing pixel is now the world's biggest entertainment industry.

moments.title: ARPANET first message
moments.body: The first message sent over ARPANET is 'lo' (the system crashed before 'login' finished).
moments.takeaway: The internet began as a military research project.

moments.title: Yahoo and Amazon launch
moments.body: Within months, Yahoo and Amazon launch, defining web 1.0 commerce.
moments.takeaway: 1995 was the year the consumer web arrived.

moments.title: Google founded
moments.who: Larry Page and Sergey Brin, Stanford
moments.body: PageRank reshapes web search. Google's ad business will reshape global media economics.
moments.takeaway: Search infrastructure became media infrastructure.

now.title: Web today
now.body: Web 2.0 platforms dominate; web 3.0 visions remain contested. Generative AI changes search.
now.open_questions: What replaces search and browsing as the default web interaction?

items.reflection: The web's first generation of companies became its incumbents.

moments.title: Instagram launches
moments.body: The photo-sharing app reaches 1 million users in two months and is acquired by Facebook in 2012.
moments.takeaway: Visual social media changed how a generation documents itself.

moments.title: TikTok launches internationally
moments.body: Douyin (2016) and TikTok internationally use algorithmic 'For You' feeds.
moments.takeaway: Algorithm-led feeds redirected what we see.

moments.title: US TikTok divestiture law
moments.body: Congress passes a law requiring ByteDance to divest TikTok or face a US ban, signed by President Biden.
moments.takeaway: Geopolitics reshape platform markets.

now.title: Short video today
now.body: Short-form video is the dominant attention format. Creator economies sustain millions of jobs.
now.open_questions: What is the next attention format after short video?

items.reflection: Algorithms now choose more of what we watch than people do.

moments.title: Netflix founded
moments.who: Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph, California
moments.body: Netflix begins as a DVD-by-mail rental company.
moments.takeaway: Media companies often pivot multiple times before success.

moments.title: House of Cards
moments.body: Netflix's first major original series, released all at once, demonstrates 'binge watching'.
moments.takeaway: Release strategy shapes viewing habits.

moments.title: Disney+ launches
moments.body: Disney+ reaches 10 million subscribers in 24 hours, beginning the streaming wars era.
moments.takeaway: Vertical integration returned with Disney's content library.

now.title: Streaming now
now.body: Ad-supported tiers, password sharing crackdowns and live sports rights shape current streaming strategy.
now.open_questions: How many streaming services can each household sustain?

items.reflection: Streaming flipped TV from broadcast to library, and back again.

moments.title: Pizzagate
moments.body: Conspiracy theories about a Washington pizzeria culminate in an armed man entering the restaurant.
moments.takeaway: Online misinformation can have offline consequences.

moments.title: Brexit and US election
moments.body: Both campaigns are accompanied by widespread misinformation; targeted micro-advertising is heavily used.
moments.takeaway: Platform-mediated campaigns reshape elections.

moments.title: 'Post-truth' word of the year
moments.body: Oxford selects post-truth as its 2016 word of the year.
moments.takeaway: Lexicographers track political climate.

now.title: Mis/disinformation today
now.body: Generative AI accelerates fake-image and fake-voice misinformation. Fact-checking networks have expanded but reach less audience than the falsehoods.
now.open_questions: Can democracies maintain shared facts in a fragmented information environment?

items.reflection: Truth has always been contested; it is now contested at machine speed.

moments.title: Ofcom established
moments.body: Ofcom consolidates broadcasting, telecoms and spectrum regulation.
moments.takeaway: Convergence of media required convergence of regulators.

moments.title: GDPR in force
moments.body: The General Data Protection Regulation reshapes how all online services handle personal data.
moments.takeaway: Privacy regulation became global through extraterritorial reach.

moments.title: Online Safety Act
moments.body: The act creates duties of care for platforms hosting user content.
moments.takeaway: Platform regulation has shifted from light-touch to statutory.

now.title: Media regulation today
now.body: EU Digital Services Act, AI Act and similar laws shape platform behaviour. Enforcement remains a moving target.
now.open_questions: Can national regulation work for global platforms?

items.reflection: Media regulation has accelerated as media power has consolidated.

moments.title: YouTube founded
moments.who: Steve Chen, Chad Hurley, Jawed Karim, California
moments.body: YouTube goes live in February 2005; the first video is 18 seconds at a zoo.
moments.takeaway: Major platforms are born banal.

moments.title: Vlogbrothers begin
moments.body: The Greens' daily video project pioneers personality-driven YouTube communities ('Nerdfighters').
moments.takeaway: Creator communities formed around individual personalities.

moments.title: MrBeast at 100 million subscribers
moments.body: MrBeast becomes one of the most-subscribed YouTubers, with elaborate stunt videos and philanthropic spin-offs.
moments.takeaway: The creator economy now matches studio scale.

now.title: Creator economy
now.body: Platforms compete on creator tools. AI-generated content threatens the human creator economy.
now.open_questions: Will individual creators sustain audiences against AI-generated competition?

items.reflection: The biggest media stars of the 2020s often began alone in bedrooms.

moments.title: Deepfakes emerge
moments.body: Face-swapping algorithms appear, originally used for celebrity impersonations.
moments.takeaway: Synthetic media has been with us since the late 2010s.

moments.title: ChatGPT launched
moments.body: ChatGPT reaches 100 million users in two months, the fastest consumer adoption in history.
moments.takeaway: Generative AI entered mass media use in weeks.

moments.title: Sora announced
moments.body: Sora generates one-minute video from text prompts, raising new questions for film and television.
moments.takeaway: Synthetic video is now a public technology.

now.title: AI media today
now.body: Watermarking standards (C2PA), AI election rules and copyright cases continue. Public trust in images is being renegotiated.
now.open_questions: What proof of authenticity will we need for media in the next decade?

items.reflection: Audiences have always negotiated with new media technologies; now the negotiation is daily.

moments.title: MP3 format published
moments.body: MP3 audio compression makes digital music files small enough to share online.
moments.takeaway: File formats can become media events.

moments.title: iPod launched
moments.body: '1,000 songs in your pocket' reshapes personal music libraries.
moments.takeaway: Devices that combine hardware, software and service can rewrite markets.

moments.title: Spotify launches
moments.body: Streaming replaces download as the dominant model within a decade.
moments.takeaway: Successive technologies disrupted each other rapidly.

now.title: Music distribution today
now.body: Streaming is the dominant model, with ongoing royalty disputes.
now.open_questions: What follows streaming?

items.reflection: A compression algorithm patented in Germany reshaped global music industry.

moments.title: Distinction published
moments.body: Bourdieu's study shows how cultural tastes correlate with social class.
moments.takeaway: Media consumption reflects and reproduces class.

moments.title: Forms of Capital essay
moments.body: Bourdieu distinguishes economic, cultural and social capital.
moments.takeaway: Cultural theory gave us new units of social analysis.

moments.title: Influencer capital
moments.body: Scholars apply Bourdieu's concepts to social media influence.
moments.takeaway: Old theory keeps finding new applications.

now.title: Cultural capital now
now.body: Platforms make some forms of cultural capital newly visible (followers, engagement) and others invisible.
now.open_questions: How do we measure cultural capital when platforms quantify it differently?

items.reflection: What you watch and share is read as who you are.

moments.title: PewDiePie's first video
moments.body: PewDiePie begins uploading gaming videos. By 2013 he is YouTube's most-subscribed channel.
moments.takeaway: Top creators can build careers in bedrooms.

moments.title: Twitch.tv launches
moments.body: Twitch (spun off from Justin.tv) becomes the dominant live-streaming platform for gaming.
moments.takeaway: Live streaming created its own media economy.

moments.title: Streaming labour disputes
moments.body: Streamers organise over revenue splits, content moderation and platform algorithmic changes.
moments.takeaway: Creator labour begins to organise.

now.title: Live streaming today
now.body: Parasocial relationships shape how viewers relate to streamers. AI VTubers add another layer.
now.open_questions: How does parasocial intimacy scale with audience size?

items.reflection: Watching strangers play games became one of the largest media categories.
